1.note: The author is concluding the story of the census, the plague, and David’s intercession for the Israelites by quoting something that David said at the end of this story. (What he said indicated an important future result of these events, which the author describes in the following chapters.) Use a natural way in your language to conclude a story. Alternate translation: [As a result of everything that had happened, David said]

David is speaking of the temple he wants the Israelites to build for Yahweh as if it were actually going to be a physical **house** in which Yahweh would live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [it will be the temple of Yahweh]

2.note: The author is using the possessive form to describe **stones** that were characterized by **hewing**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [stones that they would cut into shape]

3.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he prepared bronze]

The author does not mean that David prepared this **bronze** without weighing any of it. He means that in the end, there was too much to weigh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. The UST models one way to do that.

3.q: וַ⁠עֲצֵ֥י אֲרָזִ֖ים לְ⁠אֵ֣ין מִסְפָּ֑ר כִּֽי הֵ֠בִיאוּ הַ⁠צִּֽידֹנִ֨ים וְ⁠הַ⁠צֹּרִ֜ים עֲצֵ֧י אֲרָזִ֛ים לָ⁠רֹ֖ב לְ⁠דָוִֽיד
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since the Sidonians and the Tyrians brought trees of cedar to David to abundance, trees of cedar without number]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he prepared trees of cedar]

5.note: In this instance, the author is using the term **said** to introduce what David was thinking or saying to himself. David did not necessarily say this out loud to anyone. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing what people say to themselves or think. Alternate translation: [And David said to himself] or [And David thought]

Here David is speaking as if Solomon were like a newly growing plant whose stalk was **tender**. He means that Solomon lacks experience. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and green] or [and inexperienced]

David is using **to above** as a common expression of his culture to intensify the preceding idea. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [must be the height of greatness] or [is one that we must make very great]

The words **name** and **splendor** together express a single idea. The word **splendor** tells for what the temple will have a **name** or reputation. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [so that it will be renowned for its splendor]

The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [prior to his death]

7.note: David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the expression **my heart** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting what he wanted to do with what Solomon will be able do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for me, it was with my heart]
Here and in verses 8, 10, and 19, Yahweh’s **name** represents his “reputation.” Alternate translation: [to honor the reputation of]

8.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֨י עָלַ֤⁠י דְּבַר־יְהוָה֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר דָּ֤ם לָ⁠רֹב֙ שָׁפַ֔כְתָּ וּ⁠מִלְחָמ֥וֹת גְּדֹל֖וֹת עָשִׂ֑יתָ לֹֽא־תִבְנֶ֥ה בַ֨יִת֙ לִ⁠שְׁמִ֔⁠י כִּ֚י דָּמִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים שָׁפַ֥כְתָּ אַ֖רְצָ⁠ה לְ⁠פָנָֽ⁠י
8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [But the word of Yahweh was to me, telling me that I had shed blood to abundance, and I had made great wars. I should not build a house for his name, for I had shed much blood on the earth to his face]

When David that **the word of Yahweh was to me**, he is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh spoke a message to him. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh spoke a message to me]

8.q: דָּ֤ם לָ⁠רֹב֙ שָׁפַ֔כְתָּ וּ⁠מִלְחָמ֥וֹת גְּדֹל֖וֹת עָשִׂ֑יתָ
8.note: Yahweh is describing one event after describing another event that happened as a result of it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the opposite order. Alternate translation: [You have made great wars, and have shed blood to abundance]

8.q: לֹֽא־תִבְנֶ֥ה בַ֨יִת֙ לִ⁠שְׁמִ֔⁠י כִּ֚י דָּמִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים שָׁפַ֥כְתָּ אַ֖רְצָ⁠ה לְ⁠פָנָֽ⁠י
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you have shed much blood on the earth to my face, you shall not build a house for my name]

Here, David making **much blood** fall onto the **earth** represents David and his army killing many enemy soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you have killed many people]
Here, the **face** of Yahweh represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my presence]

9.q: הִנֵּה־בֵ֞ן נוֹלָ֣ד לָ֗⁠ךְ ה֤וּא יִהְיֶה֙ אִ֣ישׁ מְנוּחָ֔ה וַ⁠הֲנִח֥וֹתִי ל֛⁠וֹ מִ⁠כָּל־אוֹיְבָ֖י⁠ו מִ⁠סָּבִ֑יב כִּ֤י שְׁלֹמֹה֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה שְׁמ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠שָׁל֥וֹם וָ⁠שֶׁ֛קֶט אֶתֵּ֥ן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּ⁠יָמָֽי⁠ו
9.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this so that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh told me that a son would soon be born to me. He, he would be a man of rest. And Yahweh would give rest to him from all of his enemies from around. For Solomon would be his name, and he would give peace and quietness to Israel in his days]

People of this culture would commonly say **Behold** before a reference to a person and an action to mean that the person was about to do that action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A son is about to be born to you] or [A son will soon be born to you]

The expression **being born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You are about to have a son] or [You will soon have a son]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the expression **he will be** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting how David had “made great wars” with the way his son will be a **man of rest**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for him, he will be a man of rest]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **man** who will be characterized by **rest**. The next sentence makes clear that this means he will not fight wars with surrounding enemy countries. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who does not fight wars]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [In fact,]
Yahweh is able to assume that David will know that the name **Solomon** sounds like the word for **peace**. You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **quietness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and I will make Israel a peaceful and quiet place]

The terms **peace** and **quietness** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great peace]

Yahweh is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the reign of Solomon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during his reign]

9.q: הִנֵּה־בֵ֞ן נוֹלָ֣ד לָ֗⁠ךְ ה֤וּא יִהְיֶה֙ אִ֣ישׁ מְנוּחָ֔ה וַ⁠הֲנִח֥וֹתִי ל֛⁠וֹ מִ⁠כָּל־אוֹיְבָ֖י⁠ו מִ⁠סָּבִ֑יב כִּ֤י שְׁלֹמֹה֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה שְׁמ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠שָׁל֥וֹם וָ⁠שֶׁ֛קֶט אֶתֵּ֥ן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּ⁠יָמָֽי⁠ו
9.note: If you have been translating this so that there will not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh told me that he, he would build a house for my name. And he, he would be a son to Yahweh, Yahweh would be a father to him. And he would establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel to forever]

10.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **He** separately, even though the expression **he will build** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting what Solomon will do with what David wanted to do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [He will be the one to build a house for my name] or [He will be the one to build a temple to honor my reputation]

Yahweh is stating the pronouns **he** and **I** separately, even though the expression **he will be** and the implied expression **I will be** already include those meanings. He is doing that because he is contrasting the respective roles that Solomon and he will have as **son** and **father**. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [And for his part, he will be a son to me, and for my part, I will be a father to him]

Here, Solomon’s **throne** represents his authority to rule as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his royal authority]

11.note: David is using a common expression of his culture to express his wish that Yahweh will help Solomon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 16. Alternate translation: [may Yahweh help you]

12.note: David is not using this term to indicate that what he describes are the **Only** things he wants Yahweh to do. He is using it to affirm how much he wants Yahweh to do those things. If that would not be clear to your readers, you may want to use a different connecting word in your translation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

13.note: The terms **statutes** and **judgments** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all of the laws]

The expression **be dismayed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may nothing dismay you]

14.note: David is using the term **behold** to focus Solomon’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now listen]

David is using **in my trouble** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I have taken the trouble” or “I have made the effort.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have taken the trouble to prepare] or [I have made the effort to prepare]
See how you decided to represent the value or weight of a “kikkar” in 20:2 and follow the same approach here.

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since the quantity of each is to abundance, they are without weighing]

15.note: David is saying **every** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and many people who have skills for a great variety of work]

David is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **one**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and every skillful craftsman]

16.note: David is saying that the available workers are **without number** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [There are more than enough to do what is necessary]

David is using the term **Arise** to mean that he wants Solomon to take action. He does not mean that he wants Solomon to stand up from a sitting or reclining position. Alternate translation: [Take action]

17.q: וַ⁠יְצַ֤ו דָּוִיד֙ לְ⁠כָל־שָׂרֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לַ⁠עְזֹ֖ר לִ⁠שְׁלֹמֹ֥ה בְנֽ⁠וֹ
17.note: The author is introducing the direct quotation from David that he presents in the next two verses. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [And David commanded all of the rulers of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying,]

18.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֨א יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶם֙ עִמָּ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠הֵנִ֥יחַ לָ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠סָּבִ֑יב
18.note: David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Certainly Yahweh your God is with you, and he has given rest to you from around!]
The word **you** is plural in each of these instances because David is addressing the rulers of Israel. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

Here, the **hand** of a person represents his power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into my power]

18.q: וְ⁠נִכְבְּשָׁ֥ה הָ⁠אָ֛רֶץ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י עַמּֽ⁠וֹ
18.note: The expression **has been subdued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh and is people have subdued the land to their faces]

18.q: וְ⁠נִכְבְּשָׁ֥ה הָ⁠אָ֛רֶץ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י עַמּֽ⁠וֹ
18.note: Here the phrase **to the face** is a common expression of the culture that means “in front of.” The specific sense in this context is the same as in 11:13, that Yahweh and his people have conquered the **dwellers of the land** so they are no longer able to oppose them in battle. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh and his people have conquered the land]

19.note: David is using two major components of a person, his **heart** and his **soul**, to mean the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [devote your entire beings]
See how you translated the term “seek” in 15:13. Alternate translation: [to obey Yahweh your God] or [to do what Yahweh your God wants]
See how you translated the term “arise” in 22:16. Alternate translation: [and take action]

The expression **being built** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that you will build]
